name: Clavicular's looksmaxxing philosophy

lead: Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Peters, an American streamer who became prominent in 2025 and 2026 on Kick and TikTok. His approach, called 'hardmaxxing' by followers, is a maximal template for 'ascension': a sharper face, a leaner physique and a more commanding presence.

The chain runs through an aggressive mindset, then anabolic steroids, injectable peptides, extreme dieting and bonesmashing, aimed at changing face and body. The appearance claims come from his streams and anecdote rather than trials, and medical sources describe bonesmashing as pseudoscientific.

paras: Followers treat the approach as a package: streams and clips for the mindset, a paid course that includes guides on injectable peptides, and a mix of drug use, strict dieting and physical modification. People combine it with standard looksmaxxing steps such as fitness and skincare, and results are described over months to years.

Critics, including doctors, argue the content harms young men, and bonesmashing is described by medical sources as dangerous. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says he overdosed on a livestream in 2026 after a five-drug 'pentastack'. Legal matters reported include arrests, some with charges dropped, and a September 2026 Massachusetts charge that he denies and which remains an allegation.

chain: Pursuit of a sharper face and physique
angle.text: Followers of streamer Clavicular use his approach as a template for maximal 'ascension': an aggressive mindset plus drug protocols, bonesmashing talk and extreme self-improvement aimed at a more striking face and physique. The appearance claims come from his streams and anecdote rather than trials, and medical sources have criticised the approach.

lead: Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Eric Peters, an American streamer born in December 2005 in Hoboken, New Jersey, who became one of the best-known looksmaxxing influencers through Kick and TikTok in 2025 and 2026.[1] His alias comes from the community's emphasis on clavicle (shoulder) width, and his content presents looksmaxxing as a route to becoming more attractive and successful, which he calls ascending.[1] His stated aim is to improve how people look through fitness, facial-structure work, grooming and, in the more intense end of the practice, drugs and injectables.[1]

Wikipedia describes his philosophy through a set of community terms: ascending (becoming more attractive and successful), hardmaxxing (intense and painful physical alterations), mogging (being more attractive than someone else) and frame (as in being frame-mogged).[1] He rates faces publicly, and Wikipedia reports that in a December 2025 interview he criticised the profiles of public figures using facial-structure terms such as recessed side profile and maxilla.[1] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article places him among promoters of the more extreme end of the movement and of the PSL rating scale.[2]

The practices Wikipedia attributes to his content include traditional bodybuilding and fitness training with a newer focus on facial aesthetics, anabolic steroids, testosterone, methamphetamine as an appetite suppressant, peptides, fat-dissolving injections and bonesmashing, which Wikipedia describes as pseudoscientific.[1][2] He sold a paid course, first called the Clavicular System and later Clavicular's Clan, whose guides on how to ascend include suggestions of injectable peptides.[1] His career has also included controversies, bans and legal proceedings, summarised below.

paras: He says he became interested in looksmaxxing in high school and spent much of the COVID-19 lockdowns online; he was expelled from Sacred Heart University after a short time there.[1] He has said he began testosterone injections at 14 and that he is autistic, though he has no professional diagnosis.[1]

Wikipedia reports that he tells followers to ascend and to hardmaxx, and that terms associated with him such as mogging, frame and jestermaxxing were spread online by clip accounts in early 2026.[1] He has described politics as a jester pursuit, in looksmaxxing slang a foolish use of time, according to interviews cited by Wikipedia.[1]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article distinguishes softmaxxing (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness, mewing) from hardmaxxing (steroids, peptides, growth hormone, extreme dieting, cosmetic surgery) and says that bonesmashing is often discussed but rarely practised.[2] His content is associated with the hardmaxxing end.[2]
He has said looksmaxxing is about escaping incel culture rather than being part of it, a position reported by Wikipedia from a July 2026 interview.[1]

Wikipedia lists traditional bodybuilding and fitness training, a newer focus on facial aesthetics, anabolic steroids, methamphetamine for appetite suppression, peptides, Accutane, retatrutide, nebivolol and fat-dissolving injections among the methods he has discussed or shown.[1] He says steroid use left him likely sterile.[1] Medical sources describe bonesmashing as pseudoscientific.[1] Looksmaxxing critics, including doctors, call bonesmashing and similar practices unsupported or dangerous.[2]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says that in April 2026 he overdosed during a livestream after taking a five-drug pentastack, previously revealed by Australian influencer Androgenic, and was hospitalised.[2]

By late 2025 he sold a subscription course for about 50 dollars a month, with guides on how to ascend and suggestions of peptides to inject, according to coverage cited by Wikipedia from The Independent and Intelligencer.[1]

Wikipedia cites profiles in The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, Intelligencer, Spiked and Wired.[1] The Atlantic called him the newest star of the looksmaxxing movement, Intelligencer called him something of an edgelord folk hero, and Spiked argued he is better understood as a parody of masculinity than a right-wing thought leader.[1] Rolling Stone wrote that his fixation on optimisation is inseparable from aggressive sexism.[1]

Wikipedia reports that he repeatedly used racial slurs on stream and has been accused of promoting misogyny and incel-linked ideas, which he denies, and that a November 2025 video showed him injecting his then-17-year-old girlfriend with fat-dissolving peptides; critics argue his content harms young men.[1] A December 2025 livestream incident in which he drove a vehicle into a man led to a Kick ban; he described it as self-defence.[1] Events in 2026 included an Arizona arrest on drug and fake-ID charges later dropped, a Florida battery arrest, an alligator-related charge ended by plea deal and later dropped, and a permanent YouTube ban.[1]
He faces criminal charges in Massachusetts involving a 17-year-old. He has pleaded not guilty and denies the charges, which remain allegations.[1]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article reports that commentators criticise the movement as judgmental, that researchers say its advice often relies on anecdotes rather than mainstream medicine, and that doctors have criticised bonesmashing.[2] It also notes that some men report benefits such as social affirmation.[2]

lore.intro: Clavicular's content and vocabulary are widely discussed in looksmaxxing spaces and mainstream media; the entries below describe how his philosophy is characterised, not an endorsement.[1][2]
